title: Climbing Island Peak: Full Guide
excerpt: Island Peak, 6,189 m, is a technical summit in the Everest region. The full guide: the route via Everest Base Camp, acclimatization, the headwall on a fixed rope, gear, permits and cost.
seoTitle: Climbing Island Peak (Imja Tse): Route, Gear and Cost

content.value: In the small hours of the night, in the tents of base camp at 5,100 m, climbers lace their boots, switch on their headlamps and set out for Island Peak, 6,189 m (20,305 ft). Island Peak, officially named Imja Tse, is a summit in the upper Khumbu region of Nepal, about ten kilometers from Everest, and many choose it as their first summit above 6,000 m. It requires good fitness, previous trekking and climbing experience and patient acclimatization, and its summit day includes a glacier crossing and a steep wall climbed on a fixed rope with a jumar. The climbing seasons are spring and fall, and with us it is a 20-day expedition that also passes through Everest Base Camp on the way.

Island Peak is the step between a high-altitude trek and real mountaineering. Up to base camp it is walking on trails and sleeping in teahouses, and from there come the crampons, the harness, the ice axe and the ropes. Here is what you need to know before you decide: what makes the mountain technical, how our route works day by day, why the trek to Everest Base Camp is part of the acclimatization, what happens on summit day, which gear and training you need and what the price includes.
A small peak in the shadow of Lhotse

Island Peak rises in the Imja valley, in the upper part of the Khumbu region in eastern Nepal, within Sagarmatha National Park. It is a spur of a ridge running south from Lhotse, and above it rises the huge south face of Lhotse. It got its name from members of the early Everest expeditions, who saw it from Dingboche as an island in a sea of ice.

What sets it apart from a trek is the upper part of the mountain. The way to the summit includes a steep ascent, easy rock scrambling, snow and glacier crossings, a wall of snow and ice climbed on a fixed rope, and a narrow summit ridge. We grade the climb as challenging, and it suits those who have already gained experience on treks and climbs.

The reward is the view. From the summit the south face of Lhotse is very close, and beside it you see Makalu to the east, and Ama Dablam and Baruntse to the south. Everest itself you see up close a few days earlier on our route, from Kala Patthar.

content.value: The itinerary is built in two stages. In the first you walk the classic trail of the Khumbu valley to Everest Base Camp and climb Kala Patthar. In the second you turn east into the Imja valley, to Chhukung and Island Peak Base Camp. The order is deliberate: by the time you reach the mountain, your body has spent more than a week at altitude.

content.title: ✦ The trek is the acclimatization
content.value: When you reach Island Peak Base Camp, 5,100 m, you have already slept a night at Gorak Shep, 5,140 m, and stood on Kala Patthar, 5,545 m. The trek to Everest Base Camp is part of the acclimatization for the summit.
On the way: the Khumbu valley and Everest Base Camp

From Lukla, 2,860 m, you walk up the Dudh Koshi river valley to Namche Bazaar, the Sherpa market town, and continue through Tengboche and its monastery, Dingboche and Lobuche to Gorak Shep and Base Camp. On the way there are two acclimatization days, in Namche Bazaar and Dingboche.

content.value: Throughout the trek you sleep in teahouses, the simple lodges of Nepal, in twin rooms, and three meals a day, chosen from the menu, are included in the price. Every climber has a personal porter who carries up to 25 kg, and you walk with a daypack. Internet, laundry and extra meals at the teahouses are not included, so bring some cash for them.
Up to day 10 the route is the same as our Everest Base Camp trek, and we have written a full guide to it, with a description of each stage, of life in the teahouses and of the Lukla flight.

content.value: Acclimatization: altitude sets the pace

The main risk on Island Peak is not only the technical wall but the altitude. The higher you go, the less oxygen each breath brings in, and the body needs time to adapt. The accepted rule in mountain medicine is that above 3,000 m you do not raise your sleeping altitude by more than 500 m a night, and you add a night of acclimatization for every 1,000 m of sleeping altitude gained. For some climbers even this pace is too fast, so listen to your body.

Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. When symptoms get worse despite rest at the same altitude, you descend. With us the decision to continue always belongs to the guide, and safety comes before the summit. Every group carries a pulse oximeter and a Magnus satellite device, and we monitor adaptation to altitude carefully all the way.

The itinerary is built around this principle: two acclimatization days on the way in, a night at Gorak Shep and a climb to Kala Patthar before you reach the mountain, and after the summit a descent the same day to Chhukung, 4,730 m, well below base camp. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching the summit, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.
Chhukung and base camp

On day 12 you leave Lobuche and turn into the Imja valley, to Chhukung, 4,730 m, a small village that is the last teahouse stop before the mountain. On day 13 you climb to Island Peak Base Camp, 5,100 m, and sleep there in HighAir twin tents. It is the only night of the expedition not spent in a teahouse.

Our itinerary has no night at a high camp: you set out for the summit directly from base camp. Some expeditions add a night at a high camp, at about 5,600 m, to shorten summit day. With us summit day starts at base camp, which is why it is long.
Summit day
From the tent to the glacier

Summit day starts in the small hours of the night, usually between 2 and 3 in the morning. The first hours pass by headlamp, on a trail that climbs a rocky slope and a gully where some easy rock scrambling is needed. At the top of the rocks you put on crampons, rope up and step onto the glacier. The glacier has crevasses, some of them hidden under snow, which is why you move roped together. In some seasons wide crevasses are crossed on aluminum ladders fixed over them, and conditions change from season to season.

content.caption: With helmet, headlamp, ice axe and rope, in the first light of morning

content.value: The headwall: jumar and fixed rope

At the end of the glacier rises the technical section of the mountain: a wall of snow and ice about 100 m high, 45 degrees and steeper in places, with fixed ropes on it. You climb it with a jumar, an ascender that locks onto the rope and is attached to your harness: you slide it up, take a step on your crampons and lean on it when needed. At each anchor you move from one rope to the next, always clipped in. At this altitude every step takes several breaths, and this is where fitness and practice beforehand make the difference.
The summit ridge and the descent

Above the wall a narrow, steep snow ridge leads to the summit, 6,189 m, and there too you move clipped to a rope. The wall is usually descended by rappelling down the fixed rope, with a descender attached to the harness. From there you cross the glacier back to base camp, and in our itinerary you continue the same day down to Chhukung. Summit day lasts 12 to 14 hours, and it is the longest and most demanding of all the days of the expedition.

content.title: ✦ Summit day in numbers
content.value: Departure between 2 and 3 in the morning from base camp, 5,100 m. An ascent of 1,089 m to the summit, 6,189 m, and a descent of 1,459 m to Chhukung, 4,730 m. In all, 12 to 14 hours.

content.value: Technical gear and training

On Island Peak you use basic climbing gear: ropes, a helmet, an ice axe, a harness, crampons and a jumar. Before summit day participants are trained on this gear, including climbing with a jumar on a fixed rope, and a descender is usually used for rappelling. On summit day every climber has a personal climbing guide. If you have never used a jumar or rappelled, you will gain a lot from practice at a climbing gym or a short course near home before departure, so that on the mountain the movements already feel familiar in your hands.

Personal gear, meaning clothing, footwear and climbing equipment, is not included in the price, and a full gear list is sent to every registrant after registration. A climbing gear rental kit is available for 300 dollars. The most important item is a pair of high-altitude mountaineering boots that take crampons and keep your feet warm in the cold of summit day. Before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call.
The flight to Lukla

The expedition starts and ends in Lukla, the village that is home to the airport of the Everest region. In our package the flights to Lukla and back are by plane, and they are included in the price. Lukla airport is considered one of the most challenging in the world because of its short runway, and flights stop whenever the weather does not allow them.

In the busy seasons most flights to Lukla leave from the airport at Manthali in Ramechhap district, a few hours' drive from Kathmandu, not from Kathmandu itself. In our itinerary the return flight from Lukla lands in Kathmandu or Ramechhap. If you prefer, you can fly Kathmandu–Lukla–Kathmandu by helicopter for an extra 800 dollars per person. Day 19 is a spare day in Kathmandu in case the flight from Lukla is delayed, and if it is not needed it becomes a free day in the city.
Permits, visa and insurance

To enter the area you need two permits: the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit and the entry permit of the local authority, Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality. The climb itself also requires a climbing permit from the Nepal Mountaineering Association. Its price depends on the season, and it is lower in the fall than in spring. Both entry permits and the climbing permit are included in the price of our expedition.

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, get a Nepal tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. For a 20-day trip you need the 30-day visa, which costs 50 US dollars (as of 2026) and is not included. Travel and medical insurance is not included either. Before buying a policy, check that it covers climbing up to 6,189 m, including rescue and helicopter evacuation.
When to go

Nepal has two main climbing seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. Our Island Peak expeditions depart in April and May, and in September and October. In the fall, once the rains are over, the air is usually clear and the views open, but the nights at altitude are cold. In spring the days are warmer on the lower part of the route, and clouds sometimes build up in the afternoon. In the monsoon season, in the summer months, rain and cloud stop flights to Lukla, and in winter the cold at altitude is very hard.
Island Peak or Mera Peak

If you are weighing Island Peak against Mera Peak, two of our expeditions in Nepal, you are choosing between two different ways to a first summit above 6,000 m. Mera is higher, 6,476 m, and less technical: its route crosses glaciers and snow with crampons, an ice axe and a rope, but without complex technical climbing. Our Mera expedition lasts 19 days, passes through the quiet Hinku valley and includes a night in a tent at high camp. Island Peak is lower but more technical: the glacier section is shorter, and at its end is a steep wall climbed with a jumar on a fixed rope, followed by a narrow summit ridge. Our route to it passes through Everest Base Camp.
We have written a complete guide of its own about Mera Peak: our route through the Hinku valley and summit day on the glacier.

content.value: Who it suits

Island Peak suits those who want a first summit above 6,000 m with real climbing: a glacier, a wall and ropes. The climb requires good fitness, previous trekking and climbing experience and adaptation to altitude. Previous experience on a high-altitude trek, ideally above 4,500 m, is especially important, because it shows how your body reacts to altitude and to long days. In terms of fitness, you need to be able to walk about 20 km a day and to handle a summit day of 12 to 14 hours.

A medical certificate and a health declaration are conditions for departure, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join. The best preparation is long uphill hikes with a pack on your back in the months before departure, and practice with ropes if you have no experience with them.

Good to know: the climb is led by experienced local Sherpa guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail and on the wall, is worth having. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory, and the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides.
What it costs and what is included

The Island Peak expedition costs 4,050 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Kathmandu and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, domestic flights to Lukla and back, 3 nights in a 5-star hotel in Kathmandu in a single room with breakfast, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms throughout the trek, double tents during the climb, dinners at a restaurant before and after the climb, full service at base camp with cooking gear and food for the altitude, three full meals a day throughout the climb, 2 liters of hot water a day, professional local English-speaking guides, a personal climbing guide for every climber on summit day, porters for personal gear up to 25 kg per person, showers and toilets in the teahouses where available on the route, all entry permits for the trek and the climb, a first aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, a pulse oximeter for the group, a Magnus satellite device for the group, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the climb, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear (clothing, footwear, climbing gear and summit boots), tips for guides and porters (250 dollars per person), a summit bonus for the guides (250 dollars per person), the Nepal visa (50 dollars), an extra hotel night if needed, vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet. At extra cost you can add a climbing gear rental kit (300 dollars per person), helicopter flights from Kathmandu to Lukla and back (800 dollars per person), or a single room in the teahouses (20 dollars a night).
Note that in the event of an early descent from the mountain, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra hotel nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the climber.
Island Peak with HighAir

At HighAir we climb Island Peak in spring and fall, in groups of up to 10 participants, and the success rate we publish on the mountain is 84 percent. Our itinerary is built so that the trek to Everest Base Camp serves as acclimatization for the summit: two acclimatization days, a night at Gorak Shep and a climb to Kala Patthar before you reach the mountain, and a spare day at the end.

Frequently asked questions
How many days does climbing Island Peak take?

The HighAir expedition lasts 20 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. 15 of them are spent between landing in Lukla and getting back there, including the trek to Everest Base Camp and Kala Patthar, two acclimatization days and summit day. There is also a preparation day in Kathmandu and a spare day in case of bad weather.
Do you need climbing experience to climb Island Peak?

The climb requires previous trekking and climbing experience, and experience on a high-altitude trek, ideally above 4,500 m, is especially important. On the upper part of the mountain you climb a steep wall with a jumar on a fixed rope, using crampons, an ice axe, a harness and a helmet, and before summit day participants are trained on the gear. Good fitness and a medical certificate are also required.
How much does it cost to climb Island Peak?

The HighAir expedition costs 4,050 US dollars per person, and the price includes the Lukla flights, accommodation, meals on the trek, guides, porters, entry permits and the climbing permit. Not included are international flights, insurance, personal and climbing gear, the Nepal visa (50 dollars), tips (250 dollars) and a summit bonus for the guides (250 dollars).
When is the season to climb Island Peak?

Spring and fall, before and after the monsoon. Our expeditions depart in April and May, and in September and October. In the monsoon season, in the summer months, rain and cloud disrupt the Lukla flights and the trails.
What is the difference between Island Peak and Mera Peak?

Mera is higher, 6,476 m, and less technical: its route crosses glacier and snow with crampons, an ice axe and a rope, without complex technical climbing. Island Peak, 6,189 m, is more technical: the glacier section is shorter, and at its end is a steep wall climbed with a jumar on a fixed rope. Our Island Peak route passes through Everest Base Camp and lasts 20 days, while the Mera expedition goes through the Hinku valley and lasts 19 days.
What language do the guides speak?
The climb is led by experienced local Sherpa guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains.
